summary.text: At \(n=67\), the two distinct integers \(147\) and \(2055\) both give residue sum \(67\): \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\) for powers \(2^1,\ldots,2^7\), and \(1+3+9\cdot7=67\) for powers \(2^1,\ldots,2^{11}\). Thus \(67\) occurs at least twice, so its occurrence count cannot be \(1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 m\rfloor}\bigl(m\bmod 2^k\bigr),
\]
so that A049802 at the index \(m\) has value \(F(m)\). Here \(m\bmod q\) denotes the least nonnegative residue of \(m\) modulo \(q\), and \(\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor=r\) means that \(2^r\le m<2^{r+1}\). The sequence A383327 is defined by letting \(a(n)\) be the number of indices \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\).

We disprove the proposed assertion at the listed value \(n=67\) by exhibiting two distinct indices at which A049802 equals \(67\).

First take \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\), so the defining sum has seven terms. The relevant residues are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
k&147\bmod 2^k\\ \hline
1&1\\
2&3\\
3&3\\
4&3\\
5&19\\
6&19\\
7&19
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, the first four entries follow directly by division by \(2,4,8,16\); for the last three, one may use \(147=128+19\), noting also the appropriate multiples of \(32\), \(64\), and \(128\). Consequently,
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]
Thus \(147\) is one occurrence of \(67\) in A049802.

Now take \(m=2055\). We have
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
so \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). Since
\[
2055=2048+7
\]
and \(2048\) is divisible by \(2^k\) for every \(1\le k\le11\), the residue of \(2055\) modulo \(2^k\) is the same as the residue of \(7\) modulo \(2^k\). Hence
\[
2055\bmod2=1,\qquad 2055\bmod4=3,
\]
and
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7\quad\text{for every }3\le k\le11.
\]
There are nine integers \(k\) from \(3\) through \(11\), so
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=4+63=67.
\]
Thus \(2055\) is a second occurrence of \(67\) in A049802.

The indices \(147\) and \(2055\) are distinct. Therefore the set of indices \(m\) satisfying \(F(m)=67\) has at least two elements, and hence
\[
a(67)\ge2.
\]
In the finite counting formulation used for \(a(67)\), indices are searched over \(0\le m<2^{68}\). Both witnesses lie in that range: indeed,
\[
147<2055<4096=2^{12}<2^{68}.
\]
Thus the same conclusion \(a(67)\ge2\) follows directly from that formulation as well. In particular, \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\) belongs to the set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts that \(a(n)=1\) for every member of this set, so it asserts in particular that \(a(67)=1\). This contradicts the two distinct occurrences just constructed. Therefore the conjecture is false.
